sections.history: Tiruchengode, in today's Namakkal district, lies in the Kongu country and is counted among the seven Kongu Nadu shrines praised in the Tevaram, which makes it a Paadal Petra Sthalam. The hymns call the place Kodimada Chengunrur, and the child-saint Sambandar is remembered as having sung of the Lord of the red hill. The hill is older in song than in stone: the early Tamil epic Silappadikaram already refers to it as Neduvelkunru, and tradition has given it many names, among them Nagagiri, Chemmalai and Panimalai. The shrine has grown over the centuries through the patronage of later rulers, and its present stonework is medieval and after, though the exact founding of the structural temple is not firmly documented. Today it is one of the best-loved pilgrimage places of the Kongu country, and its name, the red hill, has become the name of the town itself.
sections.architecture: The temple is Dravidian in style and crowns a rocky hill whose reddish stone gives the town its name, Chengodu, the red hill. Pilgrims climb on foot by a long stairway, counted at about 1,156 steps in some sources and near twelve hundred in others, and a motor road also reaches the summit. Along the ascent a great serpent, some sixty feet long, is carved into the rock, recalling the Nagagiri, the serpent hill, of the Tevaram. At the top the sanctum holds Ardhanareeswarar, the Lord who is half Shiva and half the goddess in a single body, a rare form among the temples of the south. Beside it on the same hill stand the shrine of Senkottu Velavar, as Murugan is worshipped here and sung by Arunagirinathar, and the Vishnu shrine of Adhikesava Perumal, so that the hill gathers three streams of devotion in one place. The tall northern gopuram is attributed in one source to the early sixteenth century.
sections.legends: The hill's oldest story is of the serpent. Adisesha and the wind-god Vayu are said to have contested which of them was the mightier, and when Vayu's blast tore the great serpent loose from Mount Meru, fragments of its body fell to the earth in three places and reddened the ground with its blood; the red hill of Tiruchengode, Nagagiri, is remembered as one of them. The second story is the temple's meaning. The goddess is recalled as having sought, through her devotion, to be united with her Lord, and Shiva granted her a share of his own body, appearing as Ardhanari, half man and half woman. For this reason the place is held to teach that Shakti and Shiva are one, neither complete without the other. Couples come here to pray for harmony in their marriage and for children.
sections.festivals: The temple's best-known festival is Vaikasi Visakam, in May or June, the great celebration of the hill. In the month of Margazhi (December–January) the emerald lingam kept here is shown to devotees in the early morning hours, a darshan reserved for that season, and it is also shown during the midday worship. Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are observed as at every Shiva temple, and the worship of Murugan at the Senkottu Velavar shrine has its own days of festival. Confirm dates and timings locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Choose how you will climb. The stairway is the traditional way, taken slowly, with pauses beside the carved serpent, and the motor road is there for those who cannot manage the steps. Go early if you can, before the heat, so that the climb is cool and the town lies quiet below. At the summit you stand before Ardhanareeswarar, the Lord and the goddess in one form, and many couples sit a while in silence here. Take time also for the shrines of Senkottu Velavar and Adhikesava Perumal before you descend. Bring water and unhurried time, for the hill asks for patience and rewards it.

visit.timings: Typically open from about 6 a.m. into the afternoon and again from late afternoon until about 8:30 p.m., with a midday break; sources differ, so confirm timings locally, especially on festival days and for the early-morning Margazhi darshan.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the foot of the hill or at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and open areas of the hill, but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Tiruchengode is in Namakkal district, with frequent buses from Erode, Salem and Namakkal. The nearest railway stations are Erode Junction (about 20–25 km), Namakkal (about 30 km) and Salem Junction (about 36 km); Salem airport is around 50 km away. The temple stands on the hill above the town, reached by the stairway from the base or by the motor road.
